examinerBank.question: Walk me through your approach to this patient's breathlessness — what is your differential and how do you work through it?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: First confirm this is a cardiac/heart failure syndrome — orthopnoea, PND, bilateral oedema all support this. Then exclude the commonest causes of impaired LV function in this population: ischaemic and hypertensive heart disease (no risk factors or anginal history here, argues against), and rheumatic valvular disease (no rheumatic fever history, murmur is functional not primary valvular). Then characterise the functional pattern clinically — displaced diffuse hypodynamic apex, S3, functional MR point to a dilated/systolic pattern rather than hypertrophic or restrictive. Then screen for reversible/toxic causes — his HIV status with interrupted ART and low CD4 is the standout driver, with alcohol as a possible contributor. Also consider TB pericardial disease as a differential given his HIV status but his signs (displaced apex, no Kussmaul, no pericardial effusion) argue against it. Confirm with ECG, CXR, then echocardiogram as the definitive test.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants a structured framework-driven answer: confirm HF syndrome, exclude common causes, characterise pattern, screen for reversible causes, confirm with imaging — not a diagnosis blurted out first.

examinerBank.question: Explain the pathophysiology behind this patient's displaced, hypodynamic apex beat and the S3 you heard.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: In dilated cardiomyopathy, sarcomeres are added in series rather than in parallel, causing the ventricular chamber to dilate while the walls thin (eccentric hypertrophy). This enlarges and shifts the apex beat laterally and inferiorly, and because contractile force is reduced, the impulse is diffuse and hypodynamic rather than forceful. The S3 arises because rapid early diastolic filling occurs into a ventricle that is already volume-overloaded and non-compliant for its dilated size, generating a low-frequency vibration.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants mechanistic explanation (sarcomeres in series, eccentric hypertrophy, volume overload) not just a restatement of the finding.

examinerBank.question: His CD4 comes back at 146 with a detectable viral load. How does this change your management plan?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: CD4 <200 means he needs co-trimoxazole preventive therapy against PJP. The detectable viral load confirms non-adherence rather than treatment failure on a new regimen, so the priority is re-linking him to HIV care and restarting his existing ART regimen (TLD) with adherence counselling and addressing the psychosocial barrier that led to interruption, rather than switching regimens. He should also be screened for other opportunistic infections given this level of immunosuppression. His heart failure and HIV management must be integrated and followed up together.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants CD4 threshold application (co-trimoxazole), correct interpretation of detectable VL as adherence issue not resistance, and integrated follow-up planning.

examinerBank.question: Why would you be cautious about giving a beta-blocker to this patient today, and when would you introduce it?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: He is currently acutely decompensated with tachycardia, hypotension-borderline BP (98/64), and active fluid overload — starting a beta-blocker now could worsen acute pump failure by further reducing contractility and cardiac output. Beta-blockers should only be introduced once he is euvolaemic and haemodynamically stable on decongestive therapy, then up-titrated slowly as tolerated, alongside ACE inhibitor and spironolactone, as part of standard HFrEF therapy.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants recognition of timing/sequencing in HFrEF pharmacotherapy — decongest first, beta-blocker only once stable, not during acute decompensation.

examinerBank.question: He asks you if this is 'permanent' — what determines his long-term prognosis and what would prompt you to refer for device therapy?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Prognosis depends heavily on whether the underlying driver (HIV viraemia/non-adherence, possible alcohol contribution) can be reversed with treatment — some HIV-associated DCM improves substantially with viral suppression and ART adherence plus optimal HF therapy. He needs a repeat echocardiogram in 3-6 months after optimisation; if his LVEF remains ≤35% despite optimal medical therapy (ACEi, beta-blocker, MRA at target doses) he should be referred for consideration of ICD for sudden death prevention, or CRT if there is significant dyssynchrony/broad QRS.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants understanding that HIV-DCM can be partially reversible with ART adherence, plus correct EF threshold and timing for device therapy referral.

framework: dyspnoea/heart failure syndrome → confirm cardiac cause → exclude ischaemic/hypertensive/valvular → characterise functional pattern (dilated vs hypertrophic vs restrictive) → screen reversible/toxic causes (HIV, alcohol, peripartum) → ECG/CXR → echocardiogram (key) → risk-stratify arrhythmia/thromboembolism → treat cause + HF syndrome

patient.name: Sibusiso Mkhize
patient.occupation: security guard at a shopping centre in Pinetown
patient.personality: stoic, downplays breathlessness as 'just tired from work', becomes more forthcoming when asked directly about HIV and alcohol
patient.openingLine: Doctor, I can't even walk to the taxi rank anymore without stopping to catch my breath.

presentingComplaint: progressive shortness of breath and leg swelling over 2 months

history.fact: Breathlessness started about 2 months ago, initially only on exertion, now present on minimal activity like dressing himself
Sleeps propped up on 3 pillows; if he lies flat he wakes up gasping for air
Wakes suddenly at night choking for breath, has to sit on the edge of the bed and open a window
Notices his shoes feel tight by the end of the day; ankles and lower legs are swollen, worse in the evenings
Occasional fluttering in the chest, especially when lying on his left side, no associated blackout
No fainting or blackout spells, no loss of consciousness
No chest pain, no pressure or tightness in the chest, no pain radiating to the arm or jaw
Diagnosed HIV positive 6 years ago; was on ART but stopped taking tablets about 8 months ago after moving house and losing his clinic file, has not gone back yet
Does not know his last CD4 count or viral load, thinks it was 'okay' when he last checked over a year ago
Drinks beer most weekends with colleagues, about 6-8 quarts over a weekend, has done so for years but denies daily heavy drinking
No cough, no night sweats, no weight loss, no known TB contact
No known hypertension or diabetes, has never had a heart attack or stroke, no rheumatic fever as a child
Not currently on any chronic medication apart from occasional paracetamol; not on ART currently as above
Lives in Pinetown with his girlfriend and one child; works night shifts as a security guard; smokes occasionally, about 2-3 cigarettes a week with friends
No family history of sudden death, no relatives with known heart problems at a young age
No fevers, no joint pains, no rash, no recent diarrhoea, appetite normal, no cocaine or recreational drug use

examination.general: Mildly dyspnoeic at rest, able to speak in full sentences. No pallor, no cyanosis, no clubbing. Mild bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin. No lipodystrophy noted.
examination.respiratory: Bibasal fine crackles extending one-third up both lung fields, dull to percussion at both bases consistent with small effusions
examination.cardio: JVP raised 4cm above the sternal angle. Apex beat displaced to the anterior axillary line in the 6th intercostal space, diffuse and hypodynamic. Soft pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla (functional mitral regurgitation). Third heart sound (S3) gallop present. Pulse low-volume, regular but tachycardic.
examination.abdo: Tender smooth hepatomegaly 3cm below the costal margin, mild ascites suspected on shifting dullness, no splenomegaly
examination.neuro: Alert and orientated, no focal deficits, no signs of stroke

investigations.name: Echocardiogram
investigations.result: Dilated left ventricle (LVEDD 6.4cm), global hypokinesia, LVEF 28%, moderate functional mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, no significant valvular stenosis, no pericardial effusion, no intracardiac thrombus seen

investigations.name: HIV ELISA / rapid test
investigations.result: Positive (patient already known positive; confirms current status)

investigations.name: ECG
investigations.result: Sinus tachycardia, poor R-wave progression, non-specific ST-T wave changes, no pathological Q waves, no LVH voltage criteria

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio 0.58), upper lobe venous diversion, bilateral small pleural effusions, no pericardial calcification

investigations.name: Urea & electrolytes
investigations.result: Urea 8.9 mmol/L, creatinine 118 µmol/L, Na 133 mmol/L (mild dilutional hyponatraemia), K 4.2 mmol/L

investigations.name: Liver function tests
investigations.result: Mildly elevated GGT 68 U/L, AST 52 U/L, ALT 40 U/L, congestive hepatopathy pattern with normal bilirubin

investigations.name: Sputum GeneXpert MTB/RIF
investigations.result: Not indicated — no TB symptoms; not sent

pathophys.exertional dyspnoea and orthopnoea: Reduced systolic contractile force from a dilated, thin-walled ventricle lowers stroke volume/cardiac output; the failing left ventricle transmits raised filling pressure backwards into the pulmonary circulation, causing pulmonary venous congestion that worsens when lying flat as venous return increases
pathophys.paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea: Nocturnal reabsorption of dependent oedema fluid increases venous return and preload beyond what the dilated failing ventricle can accommodate, producing a surge in pulmonary capillary pressure and acute pulmonary oedema during sleep
pathophys.bilateral leg oedema and hepatomegaly: Chronic left heart failure raises pulmonary pressures which back up into the right heart, causing right ventricular failure with elevated systemic venous pressure, hepatic congestion and dependent interstitial fluid transudation
pathophys.displaced, hypodynamic, diffuse apex bea: In DCM, sarcomeres are added in series causing chamber dilation with wall thinning (eccentric hypertrophy); the enlarged, poorly contractile ventricle shifts the apex laterally and inferiorly and weakens the palpable impulse
pathophys.functional mitral regurgitation murmur: Progressive LV dilation stretches the mitral annulus and displaces the papillary muscles, preventing coaptation of otherwise structurally normal mitral leaflets during systole
pathophys.third heart sound (S3): Rapid early diastolic filling into a ventricle that is already volume-overloaded and has reduced compliance for its dilated size generates a low-frequency vibration audible as S3
pathophys.palpitations: Myocardial stretch and fibrosis from chamber dilation disrupt normal conduction pathways, predisposing to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias including atrial fibrillation

staging: WHO HIV clinical stage 3 (advanced immunosuppression, CD4 146, detectable viral load on interrupted ART); NYHA functional class III heart failure

immediate: Sit patient upright, give supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 >94%
IV furosemide for decongestion, monitor urine output and renal function
Continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia given tachycardia and dilated ventricle
Daily weights and strict fluid balance
definitive: Re-initiate ART promptly (TLD regimen) once stable — reintroduce with adherence counselling and address the barrier that led to interruption

Standard HFrEF therapy: ACE inhibitor (or ARB if intolerant) up-titrated as BP allows, beta-blocker introduced once euvolaemic and haemodynamically stable, spironolactone (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist)
Loop diuretic continued for ongoing congestion, titrate to lowest effective dose
Anticoagulation consideration if atrial fibrillation develops or mural thrombus found on repeat echo
Counsel regarding alcohol reduction as a contributing/aggravating factor
supportive: Restart HIV care linkage — CD4/viral load monitoring, adherence counselling, treatment supporter
Dietary sodium and fluid restriction advice
Cardiac rehabilitation and graded return to activity once compensated
Screen for and treat any intercurrent opportunistic infection
followUp: Repeat echocardiogram in 3-6 months to reassess EF and consider ICD/CRT referral if EF remains ≤35% despite optimal therapy
HF clinic follow-up with up-titration of beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor to target doses
Routine HIV clinic follow-up with viral load suppression monitoring
U&E monitoring after diuretic and ACE inhibitor initiation/titration

stationChecklist.item: Introduces self, confirms patient identity, establishes rapport and consent
Confirms the presenting problem is a cardiac/heart failure syndrome (orthopnoea, PND, oedema, exertional dyspnoea) before naming a cardiomyopathy
stationChecklist.answer: Progressive exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea on 3 pillows, PND, bilateral ankle swelling
stationChecklist.why: Framework step 1 — must establish HF syndrome before attributing to a specific cardiomyopathy

stationChecklist.item: Screens for and excludes common secondary causes: ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, valvular/rheumatic disease
stationChecklist.answer: No chest pain, no known hypertension or diabetes, no rheumatic fever history
stationChecklist.why: Framework step 2 — hypertensive/ischaemic and RHD are the commonest causes of impaired LV function in KZN and must be excluded first

stationChecklist.item: Screens for reversible/toxic causes: alcohol quantity and duration, cocaine, chemotherapy, pregnancy/postpartum timing
stationChecklist.answer: Weekend beer drinking for years; no cocaine; male patient so pregnancy not applicable
stationChecklist.why: Framework step 4 — reversible causes must be actively sought and addressed

stationChecklist.item: Establishes HIV status, ART regimen and adherence, last known CD4/viral load
stationChecklist.answer: HIV positive 6 years, ART interrupted 8 months ago, CD4 and viral load unknown to patient
stationChecklist.why: Her notes emphasise HIV cardiomyopathy is multifactorial (direct viral effect, OI, ART toxicity, nutrition) — always check HIV status and ART adherence in any new DCM

stationChecklist.item: Screens for TB symptoms and contact (cough, night sweats, weight loss) to exclude pericardial TB mimicking restrictive/right heart failure picture
stationChecklist.answer: No cough, no night sweats, no weight loss, no known contact
stationChecklist.why: TB pericardial disease is a key differential in HIV-positive patients with right heart failure signs and must be actively excluded

stationChecklist.item: Screens for red flags: exertional syncope, family history of sudden death, sustained arrhythmia symptoms
stationChecklist.answer: No syncope, no family history of sudden death, occasional palpitations without blackout
stationChecklist.why: Excludes high-risk HCM/arrhythmia picture and informs risk stratification

stationChecklist.item: Performs focused cardiovascular exam: apex beat character/position, JVP, heart sounds/murmurs, peripheral pulse volume
stationChecklist.answer: Displaced diffuse hypodynamic apex, raised JVP, S3 gallop, functional MR murmur, low-volume pulse
stationChecklist.why: Characterises the functional pattern as dilated/systolic (framework step 3) via classic DCM signs

stationChecklist.item: Examines for congestion: lung bases, hepatomegaly/ascites, peripheral oedema
stationChecklist.answer: Bibasal crackles, tender hepatomegaly, ascites, bilateral pitting oedema
stationChecklist.why: Confirms biventricular failure severity and volume status guiding diuretic therapy

stationChecklist.item: Generates a ranked differential distinguishing DCM (HIV) from ischaemic/hypertensive disease, alcohol DCM, RHD, and TB pericardial disease with linked reasoning
stationChecklist.why: Symptom-to-differential reasoning is the core exam philosophy — must exclude common causes before confirming cardiomyopathy subtype

stationChecklist.item: Requests ECG and CXR then confirms with echocardiogram as the definitive test
stationChecklist.answer: Echo shows dilated LV, LVEF 28%, global hypokinesia, functional MR/TR, no pericardial effusion
stationChecklist.why: Framework step 5 — echocardiogram is the key confirmatory investigation for cardiomyopathy subtype

stationChecklist.item: Orders HIV-related workup: confirm HIV status, CD4 count, viral load
stationChecklist.answer: CD4 146 cells/µL, viral load 38,400 copies/mL detectable
stationChecklist.why: Confirms and stages the underlying systemic cause per framework step 6

stationChecklist.item: Outlines acute stabilisation (oxygen, IV diuretic, monitoring) then definitive HFrEF therapy (ACEi, beta-blocker, spironolactone)
stationChecklist.answer: IV furosemide acutely, then ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker once stable, spironolactone, loop diuretic titration
stationChecklist.why: Standard HFrEF management per SA guidelines applied to DCM

stationChecklist.item: Addresses ART re-initiation/adherence, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, and HIV care linkage as part of treating the underlying cause
stationChecklist.answer: Restart TLD with adherence counselling, co-trimoxazole given CD4 <200, HIV clinic follow-up
stationChecklist.why: Treating the underlying HIV disease is central to management of HIV-associated DCM, not just the HF syndrome
